children.text: Correct. The titration curve shows the titration of a weak base by a strong acid, as identified by the starting pH > 7 (base being titrated) and the sudden change in pH at the beginning stage (weak solution being titrated).

Incorrect. To identify the type of titration based on the shape of the titration curve, remember that there are four main types of titrations: a strong acid titrated by a strong base, a weak acid titrated by a strong base, a strong base titrated by a weak acid, and a strong base titrated by a weak acid. Note that the titrant (the solution that is added to the initial solution) is usually a strong solution. It is possible to do titrations using a weak acid or weak base for the titrant, but this type of titration is inefficient and becomes complex when titrating an initial solution that is also weak. So titrations with a weak titrant solution is not typically considered at the introductory level of chemistry.

To decide which of the four main types of titrations is shown in the curve, first decide whether the initial solution (the solution being titrated) is an acid solution (pH < 7) or base solution (pH > 7). Then decide whether the initial solution is a strong or weak solution. The difference between strong and weak is most easily identified by the shape of the curve at the beginning stage. An initial solution that is strong will show very little change in pH during the beginning stage, because the strong solution completely neutralizes the small amount of titrant being added at this stage. There is still a significant amount of strong solution remaining, so the pH does not change much, which means the curve remains relatively flat at this stage. An initial solution that is weak will show a sudden change in pH during the beginning stage, because the weak solution reacts with the small amount of titrant being added to become its conjugate species (weak acid becomes its conjugate weak base, or weak base becomes its conjugate weak acid). As a result, the newly formed weak species causes a sudden change in the pH at this stage, and the curve suddenly increases (or decreases).

Remember the titrant (the solution being added to the initial solution) must be able to neutralize the initial solution, so it must be a base when titrating an acid solution and must be an acid when titrating a base solution.
